But I found it very rich in its less obvious details: The idea of the afterlife being a bureaucratic maze, with a haphazard mixing of esoteric rituals and taking a number. We find the torso of a woman sitting on a sofa in the attitude of anyone you'd encounter in a waiting room, except that she's sitting next to her own legs. Why is she there, like that? You're a kid, so you think "I dunno, sometimes people get chopped in half." But the costume delivers the punchline: it was a magic act gone wrong. There's a quick shot, easily missed, of Adam building his own funeral into his miniature of the town. Here's what I'd lay out for a working plan:

  • [1] Define your use case

How are you going to be using the phone? This sounds like a sales pitch, but that's because it's a good tool for fitting things to people's needs. Write out a quick list of the things you'd like to do with your phone and put the most important ones at the top. Do you want a super nice camera for photography? Do you want something super durable? Do you want wireless charging? A nice big SD card for music? Use this list to help you decide what your phone should be like, then use the search function on GSM Arena to narrow your choices down.

Also be careful to note things that are intrinsic to the phone vs. things that can be replaced by external accessories. For example, if you want long battery life you don't need a large battery, you could carry a battery backup instead. If you want a durable phone you could just buy a heavy-duty case. If you want a good camera, however, no amount of accessories can change what's on the phone already.

  • [2] Decide what phone you want to use

Your S4 should be sufficient, but I can't make that decision for you. Personally I'm a huge HTC fan and I'd love to do this with an HTC One M10. In the used market, there's the HTC One M8 and their Desire models are pretty nice and have an optical trackball if you like that kind of thing. If you like small, the HTC Aria is super cute and has the optical trackball as well.

Point is, there are a ton of phones out there and even more if you're willing to open up to older phones on the used market. If you don't need the latest and greatest, there are some super cool and unique designs out there.

  • [3] Figure out how to root it

HTC hasn't always had a great relationship with allowing people to root their phones, but they're doing better. Most phones are rootable, and you typically have better chances the older they are. Kingo Root appears to be the #1 result on Google but depending on what model you have, different rooting programs may or may not work.

Once you have your model chosen, just searching for "Manufacturer Model phone root" should be all you need.

Don't buy anything until you're confident you can get it rooted.

  • [4] Install apps you want or need

Remember that list of uses we did in step one? We'll be referring to that now. Cyanogen has a lot of useful tools built right in, but if you want something specific all you need to do is find the apk file and download it. (The .apk file extension is to Android what the .exe file extension is to Windows, or the .tar.gz file extension is to Linux, or your credit card number is to Apple)

  • [5] Get everything connected and configured

If you want to use this phone as a phone, then your options will be limited based on your carrier. CDMA carriers can be picky and only want 'their' phones to be activated, but as long as the phone as a CDMA antenna and the IMEI number isn't flagged as stolen then you should be OK. GSM carriers are even easier: you just get your SIM card and pop it in, easy as pie.

Email is stupid easy to set up, but not many people know this. For your work email, talk to IT and they'll give you POP or IMAP connection numbers that are basically the "direct line" for your phone to contact their email server. This applies to pretty much any email account ever.

Calendars, Music, all this stuff isn't difficult but it's good to spend a few hours getting it all configured. If you own an S4 then you already know the first day you spent with the phone was like this. Expect to do it again, and look through some power user guides for Cyanogen to see nifty tools like spoofing your private info to creepy applications or changing your display to help reduce battery usage.

  • [6] Miscellaneous info

One application I recommend to damn near anyone is LLAMA. The app is like a controller for your phone - it uses the concept of triggers (When conditions X Y Z are true, perform actions A B C) to make your phone really transform from a generic computing device into something that feels truly smart.

Some examples of triggers I like to use:

WHEN (headphones are plugged in) THEN (open the Music app) AND (begin playing)

WHEN (connected to Bluetooth headset) AND (phone is charging) THEN (move to Car mode) AND (turn on GPS)

WHEN (battery is below 5%) AND (phone is not charging) THEN (turn on Airplane mode) AND (play an alert)

WHEN (time is between 8:00 PM and 5:00 AM) THEN (put phone in Silent mode)

I think you start to understand just how powerful something like this is. Better yet, LLAMA is able to get your fuzzy location without using GPS at all (it just listens to which cell towers you're connected to and remembers them as areas) so you can define locations as Work or Home and give them different rulesets automatically.

One of my favorite triggers ever:

WHEN (in location Work) AND (time is 5:30 PM) THEN (send text to Wife: "Hey honey, I've got to work late tonight.")
